plain_text:
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
COMMITTEE ON TEACHING AND LEARNING 
 
September 22, 2026 5:30 p.m. 
 
1. Chair Parr calls the meeting to order at 5:30 p.m. 
 
 
2. The Clerk calls the roll. 
 
 Present: Committee Members Parr, Turner, Stewart and Smith. 
  
Absent: Committee Member Georges. 
 
 
3. Public Forum  
 
There was no one present wishing to give comment during public forum. 
 
 
6. Approval of Minutes from the August 25, 2026, Teaching and Learning Committee Meeting 
  
On motion of Committee Member Turner, duly seconded by Committee Member Stewart, it was moved 
to approve the minutes of the August 25, 2026 Teaching and Learning meeting.  Committee Member 
Georges was absent. All present were in favor and the motion passed. 
  
 
7.         Presentations    
 
a. Henry J. McLaughlin, Jr Middle School ABC Report Card Presentation by Kelly Williams, 
Principal of Henry J. McLaughlin, Jr. Middle School 
 
Nicole Doherty introduced the purpose of the District's ABC plans, which establish school-level goals 
related to Attendance, Behavior, and Curriculum and identify strategies schools will use to achieve 
those goals. 
 
Assistant Principals Amy Geary and Chantel Champagne and Instructional Coaches Carey Tripp and 
Tierney Williams presented McLaughlin Middle School's ABC plan.  The team reviewed McLaughlin's 
student demographics, noting that: 
 25.53% of students have disabilities; 
 51.63% are eligible for free and reduced-price lunch;
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 2 of 17 
 
 
 4.72% are experiencing homelessness or are in foster care; and 
 22.05% are English language learners. 
 
The school reported 2025-2026 New Hampshire SAS proficiency rates of 23% in English language arts 
compared with the state average of 55%, and 14% in mathematics compared with the state average of 
44%. McLaughlin's overarching school focus is emotional, behavioral, and cognitive engagement through 
MTSS-B and MTSS-A. 
 
Attendance 
McLaughlin's attendance goal is to increase the percentage of students attending at least 90% of school 
days from 78.8% to 81.8% by the end of the 2026-2027 school year.  Key strategies include participation 
in the District's attendance pilot with Joyce Lewis and collaboration with bilingual liaisons and mental 
health agencies to address barriers to regular attendance. 
 
Behavior 
The school's behavior goal is to increase its MTSS-B Tier I systems fidelity score from 25% to 65% by 
June 2027. Strategies include: 
 Restorative conversations between students and staff; 
 Tier I student incentives, including Cougar Paws; 
 Consistent use of schoolwide expectations and language centered around being safe, respectful, 
and responsible; and 
 Regular review of conduct-referral and incentive data. 
 
They noted that overall conduct referrals increased during the prior school year, while suspensions 
decreased. It was also noted during Committee discussion that a significant portion of the increase in 
referrals was associated with implementation of the cell phone policy. 
 
Curriculum 
McLaughlin's curriculum goal is to increase overall New Hampshire SAS reading and mathematics 
proficiency by five percentage points during the 2026-2027 school year.  The school will continue state-
assessment preparation, utilize guaranteed and viable curriculum materials to strengthen academic rigor, 
and celebrate student academic growth.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 3 of 17 
 
 
The school reported several areas of improvement from 2026, including: 
 Grade 6 mathematics proficiency increased nine percentage points; 
 Grade 5 reading proficiency increased four percentage points; 
 Grade 6 reading proficiency increased five percentage points; 
 Grade 7 reading proficiency increased three percentage points; and 
 Grade 8 reading proficiency increased three percentage points. 
 
Questions and comments from the committee included: 
1. The Administration reported an average class size of approximately 25 students, with some classes 
exceeding the District's recommended maximum. Sixth-grade classes average approximately 20 
students, while fifth-grade classes generally average 21 to 22 students. 
2. The Committee congratulated McLaughlin on its academic improvements and the completion of 
its renovated school building.  
3. Administration reported that students have responded enthusiastically to the renovated facility and 
were looking forward to participating in the upcoming ribbon-cutting celebration. 
 
 
b. 2026 NH Statewide Assessment Results - Manchester – by Nicole Doherty, Assistant 
Superintendent of Elementary Schools, Teaching and Learning and Leslie Whitney, Executive 
Director of Teaching and Learning 
 
Assistant Superintendent Nicole Doherty and Executive Director of Teaching and Learning Leslie 
Whitney presented the District's 2026 statewide assessment results.  They emphasized that the District 
served 11,865 students during the assessment period, with more than half economically disadvantaged, 
more than 20% multilingual learners, and nearly 24% students with disabilities. 
 
Students in grades 3 through 8 participate in statewide reading/writing and mathematics assessments. 
Science is assessed in grades 5, 8, and 11, while grade 11 students participate in the SAT for English 
language arts and mathematics. 
 
Districtwide proficiency increased in all three assessed areas: 
 Reading and writing increased three percentage points; 
 Mathematics increased two percentage points; and
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 4 of 17 
 
 
 Science increased three percentage points. 
 
They emphasized that, although overall proficiency remains below desired levels and significant gaps 
remain between Manchester and statewide performance, the District is seeing positive movement. 
Assessment participation reached 96% in reading/writing and mathematics, exceeding the 95% federal 
expectation. Science participation was 92%. 
 
Since 2021, reading/writing proficiency has increased four percentage points and mathematics proficiency 
has increased six percentage points. Science performance has remained relatively flat over the longer 
period but increased three points during the most recent year. 
 
The Administration also reviewed subgroup performance. Reading/writing proficiency among students 
receiving special education services and English language learners remains below 10%, while 
economically disadvantaged students were at approximately 21%. Similar challenges exist in 
mathematics, with English language learners and students receiving special education services below 10% 
proficiency and economically disadvantaged students at approximately 13%. 
 
The District will continue analyzing subgroup data to evaluate access to strong core instruction, 
intervention, differentiated instruction, and other supports. 
 
Reading and writing results demonstrated improvement in grades 3, 4, and 5, as well as grades 7 and 8. 
Grade 3 increased seven percentage points and grade 5 increased eight percentage points.  They noted that 
the improvement among younger students may reflect ongoing work in curriculum implementation, 
professional learning communities, professional development, and strengthened literacy instruction. 
Mathematics also improved across several grade levels. Grade 3 increased from 26% to 32%, while 
smaller gains were seen in grades 4, 5, 7, and 11. 
 
Science proficiency increased districtwide. Grade 5 increased from 12% to 17%, grade 8 remained steady, 
and grade 11 increased one percentage point.  They highlighted individual schools and grade levels 
showing substantial year-over-year improvement. Examples included: 
 Northwest grade 3 mathematics increasing 18 percentage points; 
 Smith grade 3 mathematics increasing 15 percentage points;
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 5 of 17 
 
 
 Southside grade 5 reading/writing increasing 14 percentage points; 
 McLaughlin grade 6 mathematics increasing nine percentage points; and 
 Southside grade 7 mathematics increasing 10 percentage points. 
 
The Administration emphasized that these examples are not intended as school rankings, but rather as 
opportunities to examine instructional practices and determine what may be replicated elsewhere.  At the 
high school level, reading/writing remained relatively steady at approximately 39% proficiency.  
Mathematics increased slightly to approximately 12%, and science increased slightly to approximately 
16%. High school mathematics remains a significant area of focus. 
 
It was noted that statewide assessment results represent only one measure of high school success. 
Additional accountability information, including graduation rates, college and career readiness, and CSI, 
TSI, and ATSI designations, is expected in November.  Three areas requiring continued acceleration were 
identified: 
 Closing the achievement gap between Manchester and the state; 
 Improving middle school performance, including grade 6 reading/writing; and 
 Improving high school mathematics. 
 
The District will address these areas through existing priorities involving strong core instruction, MTSS, 
attendance and engagement, strong professional learning communities, targeted professional 
development, and consistent progress monitoring. 
 
Questions and comments from the committee included: 
1. The Committee discussed increased assessment participation, particularly at the middle and high 
school levels. Administration reported that additional emphasis on participation, along with 
changes at the high school level that allowed students to focus on the SAT and PSAT testing day, 
contributed to improved participation. 
2. Committee members requested additional analysis of schools experiencing double-digit 
proficiency increases to better understand whether instructional practices, attendance, 
implementation fidelity, student engagement, or other factors contributed to the gains.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 6 of 17 
 
 
3. The Administration has begun conversations with principals, assessment coordinators, reading 
specialists, and mathematics coaches and will gather information to identify common factors 
associated with stronger performance. 
4. The Committee also discussed the impact of subgroup populations on aggregate District 
performance. Administration is working with the District's data analysis staff to examine results 
for English language learners, students receiving special education services, and the remaining 
student population separately to provide additional context. 
5. It was noted that newly arrived English language learners may receive an exemption from the 
ELA assessment during their first year in the country but are subsequently expected to participate. 
Administration acknowledged ongoing concerns regarding the ability of state assessments alone to 
accurately demonstrate the progress of multilingual learners and noted that ACCESS testing 
provides additional information regarding English language development. 
6. The Committee discussed the use of professional learning communities as a vehicle for sharing 
successful instructional strategies across schools and grade levels. 
7. Science instruction was also discussed. Administration identified a need to ensure students 
consistently participate in hands-on laboratory experiences and are given opportunities to write 
about and communicate scientific learning. Additional professional development will emphasize 
literacy across content areas, including science-specific writing. 
8. Mathematics performance was discussed and the decline in statewide mathematics proficiency as 
students advance through grade levels. Administration noted that mathematics performance is also 
a statewide concern and that the New Hampshire Department of Education is examining 
professional development and other supports similar to work previously undertaken in literacy. 
 
 
c. Multilingual Learner Education: Department Updates – by Wendy Nassar Perron, Executive 
Director of Multilingual Learner Education and Meryl Shea, Assistant Director of Multilingual 
Learner Education 
 
Executive Director of Multilingual Learner Education Wendy Perron and newly appointed Assistant 
Director Meryl Shea presented an update on the Multilingual Learner Education Department.  Ms. Shea 
shared that she is beginning her 17th year with the District and previously served as a multilingual learner 
teacher at Southside Middle School.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 7 of 17 
 
 
The department oversees three primary areas: 
 English language development; 
 Dual Language Immersion programs; and 
 Language access services, including translation, interpretation, and multilingual liaisons. 
 
They stated that they also have two new English Language Development instructional coaches, Sarah 
Dubois and Lauren Grosse. 
 
Approximately 20% of Manchester students are identified as English learners. Approximately half of the 
District's English learner population was born in the United States in homes where a language other than 
English is spoken. 
 
The Department continued standards-alignment work associated with the core curriculum adopted in fall 
2024. Initial implementation focused on common curriculum units, while the past year focused on 
developing common performance assessments and reviewing student work. 
 
At the secondary level, the Department's primary goal is to reduce the number of multilingual learners 
failing one or more content-area courses.  The Department will continue professional development related 
to co-teaching and will collaborate with Student Services to establish uniform guidance for evaluating 
multilingual students who may also have a suspected disability. The goal is to help school teams 
distinguish between challenges associated with language acquisition and those potentially associated with 
a disability. 
 
An internal multilingual education guidebook has also been developed to provide District staff with 
consistent protocols, expectations, research, and guidance related to state and federal requirements. 
Procedures for students presenting international transcripts have been revised in collaboration with the 
Comprehensive Guidance Department to improve consistency and equity. 
 
Principals have received disaggregated data regarding multilingual learner performance on New 
Hampshire SAS and iReady assessments to assist with school-level planning.  It was reported that the 
performance gap between multilingual learners and non-multilingual peers has decreased. Average New
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 8 of 17 
 
 
Hampshire SAS score gaps were approximately 20 to 25 points, compared with more than 30 points 
previously.  The gap tends to widen at the middle school level as academic language demands increase. 
At the high school level, approximately 56% of English learners were failing one or more content courses, 
with the highest failure rates in mathematics and science. At the middle school level, approximately 13% 
were failing one or more content courses. This information will inform the Department's secondary-level 
work with instructional coaches. 
 
They also reviewed WIDA ACCESS results. WIDA is implemented updated assessments aligned to 
revised standards in 2026, the District is treating 2026 as a new baseline rather than directly comparing 
results with prior years.  The District achieved 97% participation in ACCESS testing.  The state target for 
2026 was for 57.74% of English learners to be considered on track toward proficiency. Manchester's 
overall rate was 24.28%. Administration explained, however, that approximately 50% of students within 
their first four years of programming met their individual proficiency-growth targets.   Approximately 
28% of Manchester's multilingual learners have been enrolled in the program for five years or more. Once 
students reach that point, their annual target automatically becomes the 4.5 proficiency score necessary to 
exit the program, which affects the District's overall accountability percentage even when individual 
students demonstrate significant year-over-year growth. 
 
They reported a 24% increase in the number of students who tested out of the English learner program in 
2026 compared with 2025. 
 
The District began the year fully staffed in its Dual Language Immersion programs, including 
Spanish/English programming at Bakersville and French/English programming at Weston.  The original 
Bakersville cohort has now advanced to grade 2 and is participating in the planned 70/30 language 
allocation model.  In the Spanish program, 75% of kindergarten students completed the year on grade 
level and an additional 13% above grade level in early Spanish literacy. Among the original first-grade 
cohort, 55% finished at or above grade level. 
 
They reiterated that national research indicates that students learning literacy simultaneously in two 
languages may initially appear to progress more slowly but are expected to demonstrate stronger 
performance as they move into later elementary grades.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 9 of 17 
 
 
In the French Dual Language Immersion program, 75% of students ended the year at mid-grade level or 
above in French, while 80% ended the year at mid-grade level or above in English. 
 
The District continues to provide interpretation, translation, and multilingual liaison services to support 
meaningful communication with families.  All staff receive annual training regarding language-access 
obligations and available District resources.  During the previous school year: 
 715 calls utilized the District's on-demand telephone interpretation service; 
 Multilingual liaisons provided hundreds of additional in-person calls and meetings; and 
 Approximately 280,000 messages were exchanged between home and school through 
TalkingPoints. 
 
Questions and comments included: 
1. Committee members recognized the significant expansion of multilingual services over the past 
several years, including instructional coaches, multilingual liaisons, Dual Language Immersion 
programming, TalkingPoints, and expanded interpretation and translation resources. 
2. A recent example was also shared regarding a French-speaking parent who received a ThrillShare 
notification concerning a change in meeting location and mistakenly believed she was required to 
attend the meeting. The parent was ultimately able to connect with an interpreter. The experience 
was noted as an example of the importance of continuing to examine how translated District 
communications are understood by families. 
 
8. Policy - Instruction 743 Remote and Virtual Learning – by Nicole Doherty, Assistant 
Superintendent of Elementary Schools, Teaching and Learning 
  
Assistant Superintendent Doherty presented revisions to Policy Instruction 743, Remote and Virtual 
Learning.  The policy was revised to align with updated New Hampshire Ed 306 minimum standards and 
replace the District's existing online and virtual education policy. 
 
The revised policy addresses two distinct types of learning: 
1. Remote instructional days when schools are closed because of weather or another qualifying 
circumstance; and 
2. Individual virtual learning opportunities for students, including approved online coursework, 
dual or concurrent enrollment, credit recovery, and advanced coursework.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 10 of 17 
 
 
The policy clarifies that virtual learning is not intended to replace regular school attendance for vacations, 
family travel, or temporary absences.  It also addresses District responsibilities for technology and student 
support and maintains that high school credit is awarded based on mastery of competencies rather than 
seat time. 
 
There were no questions or comments from the committee. 
 
On motion of Committee Member Turner, duly seconded by Committee Member Smith, it was moved to 
approve the revisions to policy Instruction 743: Remote and Virtual Learning and forwards this item to 
the full Board of School Committee for approval. All present were in favor and the motion passed. 
 
 
9.  New Policy - Instruction 767: Career Exploration, Readiness, Pathways and Credentialing – by 
Nicole Doherty, Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Schools, Teaching and Learning 
 
Assistant Superintendent Doherty presented new Policy Instruction 767, required as part of the updated 
New Hampshire Ed 306 minimum standards. Although the policy is new, administration explained that 
much of the work described in the policy is already occurring throughout the District.  The policy 
establishes a K-12 career-development framework reflecting Manchester's grade configuration: 
 Grades K-4: Age-appropriate career awareness; 
 Grades 5-8: Intentional career exploration; and 
 Grades 9-12: Increasingly focused career pathways connected to student interests and future goals. 
 
It was stated that within the policy, these levels need to be revised, it should read K-4, 5-8 and 9-12, 
instead of K-5, 6-8 and 9-12. 
 
Opportunities include career and technical education, extended learning opportunities, work-based 
learning, dual and concurrent enrollment, apprenticeships, and industry-recognized credentials. 
 
Questions and comments included: 
1. Committee members discussed the potential workload implications for school counselors and 
other staff responsible for helping students develop postsecondary goals and identify pathways.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 11 of 17 
 
 
2. The Administration reported that the policy had been reviewed with Director of Comprehensive 
Guidance Joyce Lewis and that much of the required work is already distributed among school 
counselors, Extended Learning Opportunity staff, dual enrollment staff, teachers, administrators, 
and existing courses and programs. 
3. Administration agreed to continue monitoring implementation and revisit the policy if additional 
clarification or adjustments become necessary. 
4. Committee Member Turner indicated that on page 91, it says the District shall but it does not 
identify who the responsible person would be.  I was asked for this to be reviewed.  Ms. Doherty 
stated that this is understood within the district but they did not want to put it into the document, 
as if that changes, the policy would need to be revised. 
 
On motion of Committee Member Stewart, duly seconded by Committee Member Turner, it was moved 
to approve the proposed NEW policy Instruction 767: Career Exploration, Readiness, Pathways and 
Credentialing, as amended, and forwards this item to the full Board of School Committee for approval. 
All present were in favor and the motion passed. 
 
 
10.   Policy Instruction 703: Curriculum Development and Instruction – by Dr. Sean Parr, Teaching and 
Learning Chair and Nicole Doherty, Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Schools, Teaching 
and Learning 
  
Assistant Superintendent Doherty presented proposed revisions to Policy Instruction 703 in conjunction 
with Policy Instruction 729. The revisions were developed to ensure District policy reflects both 
competency-based learning requirements under Ed 306 and the importance of meaningful student 
attendance and participation. 
 
Dr. Parr stated that Policy 703 strengthens expectations regarding meaningful in-person instructional 
experiences, performance assessments, and opportunities for students to demonstrate competencies. 
 
Questions and comments from the committee included: 
1. The  Committee considered language requiring meaningful instructional experiences to be 
identified on course syllabi. Members expressed concern that the language appeared to apply 
to all grades despite syllabi primarily being used at the high school level. The Committee 
agreed to remove the specific syllabus requirement and revise the provision to state that, as
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 12 of 17 
 
 
part of curriculum development or revision, each course shall include meaningful in-person 
instructional experiences. 
2. The Administration clarified that the District is continuing to build competency-based 
instruction and curriculum but is not yet moving fully to competency-based grading. 
3. The Board clerk stated that the reference to the approvals at the bottom of the document need 
to be reformatted, the font size and type should match the rest of the document and the other 
policies. 
 
On motion of Committee Member Stewart, duly seconded by Committee Member Smith, it was moved to 
approve the proposed revisions to policy Instruction 703: Curriculum Development and Instruction, as 
amended, and forwards this item to the full Board of School Committee for approval. All present were in 
favor and the motion passed. 
 
11.   Policy Instruction 729: Middle and High School Grading – by Dr. Sean Parr, Teaching and 
Learning Chair and Nicole Doherty, Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Schools, Teaching 
and Learning 
 
Dr. Parr and Ms. Doherty explained that Policy Instruction 729 works in conjunction with Policy 703 and 
addresses grading and the awarding of academic credit.  The revised policy recognizes the importance of 
attendance while also complying with Ed 306 requirements that grades and credits reflect demonstrated 
learning and achievement of competencies. 
 
Students are expected to attend school in order to access instruction, build relationships, participate in 
meaningful learning experiences, and demonstrate competencies. However, attendance alone cannot 
determine an academic grade or whether credit is awarded. 
 
There were no questions or comments on this item. 
 
On motion of Committee Member Stewart, duly seconded by Committee Member Smith, it was moved to 
approve the proposed revisions to policy Instruction 729: Middle and High School Grading and forwards 
this item to the full Board of School Committee for approval. All present were in favor and the motion 
passed.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 13 of 17 
 
 
12. Curriculum Management Plan Update – by Leslie Whitney, Executive Director of Teaching and 
Learning 
 
Executive Director of Teaching and Learning Leslie Whitney, Middle School Academic Director Tina 
Proulx, High School Academic Director Geoff Giotas, and District implementation specialists provided 
an update on Manchester's Curriculum Management Plan.  The Curriculum Management Plan is aligned 
with the District's goals, mission, and vision and establishes a systematic process for curriculum 
development, assessment, implementation, and evaluation.  The plan provides a six-year cycle intended to 
support: 
 Districtwide consistency; 
 Quality assurance; 
 Equity and accessibility; 
 Data-informed decision-making; and 
 Continuous evaluation and refinement. 
 
Two distinct processes are incorporated into the plan: curriculum cycles and program/material adoption 
cycles.  Mathematics and world languages were used as examples of content areas currently progressing 
through the cycle. 
 
Mathematics 
A K-12 mathematics investigation committee will examine current evidence-based mathematics practices, 
District and state assessment data, standards, curriculum expectations, and existing instructional 
resources.  The Teaching and Learning committee will identify areas of success and challenge and 
examine available programs and materials before developing recommendations. 
 
World Languages 
World language teachers in grades 5-12 completed the initial investigation stage during the previous 
school year and are completing the next stage of exploration and analysis. Teachers also participated in a 
pilot during the spring. Later years of the curriculum cycle focus on refining instructional practices, 
reviewing student data, continuing professional development, and determining whether adjustments are 
necessary.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 14 of 17 
 
 
The Administration emphasized that the six-year cycle does not mean the District waits six years to 
respond to concerns. Curriculum and program data are reviewed annually, and adjustments can be made 
throughout the cycle. 
 
Questions and comments from the committee included: 
1. There was discussion about the distinction between curriculum and instructional 
programs. The Administration clarified that curriculum refers to the standards and 
learning expectations established by the District, while programs such as Ready Math and 
Amplify are resources used to deliver that curriculum. If the curriculum continues to meet 
student needs, an instructional program may continue beyond the six-year cycle. 
Conversely, data may result in adjustments before the end of a cycle. 
2. Committee members recognized the importance of having a transparent and predictable 
process for curriculum and program review and noted connections between the Curriculum 
Management Plan, statewide assessment results, multilingual learner data, special 
education programming, and instructional practices. 
 
 
13. Teaching and Learning Highlights/Updates – by Nicole Doherty, Assistant    
Superintendent of  Elementary Schools, Teaching and Learning 
● Adult Education Update 
● Artificial Intelligence 
 
Assistant Superintendent Doherty provided several District updates. 
1. Artificial Intelligence 
The District's artificial intelligence policy and procedures were reviewed with staff during beginning-of-
year professional development, with an emphasis on responsible and appropriate use.  High school staff 
participated in additional professional development led by SchoolAI on September 1.  Middle school staff 
are scheduled for similar training on November 3, followed by elementary staff on March 5.   The District 
AI Committee met during the summer and again in September to review staff feedback, identify next 
steps, and develop additional resources for teachers. 
 
Executive Director Leslie Whitney was recognized for her leadership in coordinating the District's AI 
work, professional development, and staff resources.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 15 of 17 
 
 
A community forum regarding artificial intelligence in the schools is planned for December. Community 
members who have questions prior to the forum may contact Assistant Superintendent Doherty. 
 
2. Adult Education 
A more detailed Adult Education presentation will be provided at the next Committee meeting. 
Manchester Adult Education received a state allocation of $16,923 for the 2026-2027 school year. 
For comparison, the cost of the District's part-time adult education teacher during the previous year was 
approximately $17,936, meaning the entire state allocation does not cover the cost of that single position. 
Administration stated that opportunities exist to expand Adult Education programming and provide 
additional pathways for students and community members; however, meaningful and sustainable 
expansion will require additional funding. 
 
3. Constitution Day 
Ms. Doherty highlighted Constitution Day activities held throughout the District on September 17. 
Elementary students participated in activities introducing the Constitution and its importance.  Middle 
school students explored classroom constitutions, the Bill of Rights, the purpose of government, 
differences between the New Hampshire and United States constitutions, and the three branches of 
government.  High school students engaged in deeper discussions and debates regarding representation, 
federal and state power, individual rights, and the creation and defense of their own constitutions. 
 
4. Hopeville Screening 
The District will partner with the University of New Hampshire and the International Dyslexia 
Association to host a screening of Hopeville: How to Win the Reading War on October 8 from 4:00 to 
7:00 p.m.  The screening will be followed by a panel discussion regarding evidence-based reading 
instruction and how students learn to read.  District educators will also have an opportunity to participate 
in a screening and panel discussion during the October 9 professional learning day. 
 
5. Central High School Accreditation 
Administration reported that Central High School received continued accreditation following its decennial 
review by the New England Association of Schools and Colleges.  The Commission recognized several 
strengths, including: 
 The commitment of school leadership and staff to continuous improvement;
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 16 of 17 
 
 
 Celebration of Central's multicultural community; 
 Strength of the visual and fine arts programs; and 
 A culture of safety, connection, and Central pride. 
 
Areas for continued improvement include curriculum documentation and continued development of the 
school's core values, beliefs about learning, and vision of the learner.  Central will continue this work 
through its school growth and improvement plan and is expected to submit its first progress report by May 
1, 2027. 
 
The Committee congratulated Central's administration, faculty, staff, and students on receiving continued 
accreditation. 
 
14.      Upcoming Teaching and Learning Meeting Date: October 27, 2026 @ 5:30 pm 
● Beginning of the Year District Assessment Results 
● Career Pathway Update 
● Adult Education Program Update 
● Special Education Program Update 
● Fine Arts Presentation 
 
Dr. Parr stated that the next Teaching and Learning Committee meeting is scheduled for October 27, 
2026 at 5:30 p.m.  Anticipated agenda items include: 
 Central High School ABC presentation; 
 Adult Education program update; 
 Special Education program update; 
 Fine Arts presentation; 
 Career Pathways update; and 
 Beginning-of-year District assessment results, including iReady data. 
 
 
15. TABLED  ITEMS 
 
There were no tabled items. 
 
 
16.   NEW BUSINESS 
 
No committee members had any new business to present.
September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda

If there is no further business, a motion is in order to adjourn. 
 
 
On motion of Committee Member Turner, duly seconded by Committee Member Smith, it was moved to
